meta.description: The best Bible study app for iPhone in 2026 is the one built for notes, highlights, and commentaries — not just daily reading. How to pick a study app, plus the free lock-screen layer that keeps you in Scripture between sessions.

sections.title: Quick Answer
sections.content: The **best Bible study app for iPhone in 2026**, if you want real depth without a subscription, is **Blue Letter Bible** — free, ad-free, with Strong's numbers, a Greek/Hebrew interlinear, and a full commentary library with no paywall anywhere in the app. **Olive Tree** and **Logos** cover more ground for people willing to pay for it, either one resource at a time or by subscription. None of the four apps this page actually compares put Scripture in front of you between study sessions — that's a different job, and it's the one **FaithWall** (our own app) is built for.

**FaithWall is our app** — this comparison reflects that, but not by ranking it as a study tool. FaithWall has no notes, no highlights, and no lexicon, and it isn't trying to. The four apps below are ranked on their own merits for studying Scripture; FaithWall shows up afterward, honestly, for the different job of keeping a verse in view between the times you open one of them.

sections.text: This page stays focused on study-specific picks — notes, highlights, commentaries, and cross-references. Looking for the best Bible apps overall, not just study tools? See our ranked roundup of the best free Bible apps for iPhone.

About four in ten practicing Christians say AI has already helped them with prayer, Bible study, or spiritual growth, per Barna Group's 2026 State of the Church research. That's a reasonable instinct — a chat window is available at 2am and a physical commentary isn't — but a generated answer isn't the same as a cross-reference you can check yourself, a Strong's number you can trace through a lexicon, or a commentary written by a named scholar and reviewed by an editor. The four apps below still do that work better than anything generative, and none of them cost what most people assume.
Why most "best Bible study app" lists don't actually compare study features

Most Bible-app roundups list the same five names and call it a comparison. They'll tell you an app "has commentaries" or "supports highlighting" without saying which commentaries, whether they're free, or whether the highlights sync across your devices. That's not a comparison — it's a feature checklist copied from each app's own marketing page. The four questions below are the ones that actually decide which study app is worth your time, answered from what each publisher documents about its own app rather than from a generic feature list.
Which iPhone Bible app is best for taking notes?

**For most people, YouVersion is the easiest place to start taking notes on Scripture.** A free account saves highlights, notes, and bookmarks and syncs them across every device automatically, with no setup beyond signing in. Olive Tree's annotation tools go a step further: its Study Center surfaces every commentary, dictionary, and study Bible in your library that's relevant to whatever verse you're actually reading, so a note sits next to the resources that informed it. Logos organizes notes with more structure still — tagging, cross-linking between notes and passages, searchable note libraries — but that depth is built for people already committed to its subscription, not for someone deciding whether to start taking notes at all. If you already use YouVersion or Olive Tree and just want the fastest way to mark a verse, our guide to [highlighting verses on iPhone](/blog/how-to-highlight-verses-on-iphone) covers the actual tap sequence.
Which free app has Strong's numbers or an interlinear Greek and Hebrew text?

**Blue Letter Bible is the one free app on this list with real original-language tools built in.** Tap any word and its Strong's number opens the Outline of Biblical Usage, a full lexicon entry, and every other place in Scripture that Greek or Hebrew word appears — with no paywall anywhere in the app. Its interlinear view lines up the original Hebrew or Greek text against the English translation, word by word, which is the feature people usually end up paying Logos for. Olive Tree has a Strong's popup too, with an interactive graph showing how a word is translated across the whole Bible, but its deeper original-language resources are sold as add-ons rather than included free. If word-level study is the actual goal rather than a side interest, [verse mapping](/blog/verse-mapping-iphone-app) is the structured method that puts a tool like this to use.
Can you get Bible commentaries free on iPhone?

**Yes — Blue Letter Bible ships its full commentary library free, with no premium tier to unlock.** Olive Tree includes a handful of free resources with the base app, but a fuller library — a modern translation bundle, two study Bibles, a couple of commentaries — typically runs $300 to $500 over time as one-time purchases rather than a subscription, per LearnOfChrist's 2026 review of the app. Bible Gateway keeps its 200+ translations free but gates its 60-plus study tools, commentaries included, behind Bible Gateway Plus at $7.99 a month or $79.99 a year. Logos includes a few resources on its free tier, but the commentaries scholars actually cite — BDAG, TDNT, the International Critical Commentary — sit behind its $19.99-a-month Max subscription.

| App | Notes & highlights | Original-language tools | Commentaries | Price |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| YouVersion | Yes — free, syncs across devices | None (no Strong's, no interlinear) | Limited, reading-plan notes only | Free |
| Olive Tree | Yes — annotation + Study Center | Strong's popup with translation graph; deeper tools sold separately | A few free; fuller library ~$300-$500 one-time | Free app; resources priced individually |
| Blue Letter Bible | Yes — basic notes | Strong's numbers + full Hebrew/Greek interlinear | Full library, no paywall | Free, no ads, no in-app purchases |
| Logos | Yes — tagging, cross-linked note libraries | Greek/Hebrew syntax search on the Max tier | Scholarly commentaries on the Max tier | $9.99-$19.99/month |
| Bible Gateway | Yes — free account, syncs | None built in | 60+ tools via Bible Gateway Plus | Free app; Plus $7.99/mo or $79.99/yr |
For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and of spirit, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart.
Study app vs. reading app — which do you need?

**Most people need both, and they're not the same app.** A reading app like YouVersion is built for opening a chapter and getting through it — reading plans, a clean interface, translations you can swap without friction. A study app like Blue Letter Bible, Olive Tree, or Logos is built for stopping on one verse and going deep — checking what the original word meant, reading a commentator's take, following a cross-reference chain. Trying to make one app do both usually means it does neither well: a reading app's commentary is an afterthought, and a study app's reading experience is cluttered with tools you don't need for a straight read-through. Pick a reading app for daily reading and a study app for the verses that stop you — [Bible memorization apps](/blog/bible-memorization-apps-iphone) tackle a third, related job (keeping a verse after you've studied it), worth separating from both.
The realistic study stack for 2026
If you want the honest **best Bible study app iPhone 2026** answer, it isn't one app — it's three apps with clear, non-overlapping roles.

items: **A reading app for daily Scripture.** YouVersion if you want the easiest free start; see our [free-reading pick](/blog/best-free-bible-app-iphone) roundup for the full comparison of reading-first apps.

**A study app for when a verse stops you.** Blue Letter Bible costs nothing and covers Strong's numbers, the interlinear, and commentaries in one free app; Olive Tree or Logos are worth paying for once you know exactly which deeper resources you keep reaching for.
**FaithWall for the days you don't open either.** Free, on the lock screen, the piece that keeps a verse in view between the sessions where the actual studying happens.

sections.content: **The cheap test:** which of the three did you actually open this week? For daily reading it's usually whichever app needed the least setup; for study it's whichever tool answered the specific question you had. FaithWall doesn't compete on either front — it just keeps the verse in front of you while you decide.

sections.text: How to actually start this week

items: Pick one app from the comparison table based on what you actually need — Blue Letter Bible if the goal is free depth, YouVersion if the goal is just consistency.
Install **FaithWall** alongside it (free, 60 seconds, no account) so Scripture stays in view on the days you don't open either.
Set a single recurring reminder at your real quiet-time slot, not an aspirational one.
Start with one book — **John** or **Mark**, not Leviticus — so you're building a habit, not a syllabus.
Don't add a fourth app before the first three are actually in use.

sections.text: Frequently Asked Questions
Is YouVersion good enough for serious Bible study?

For reading, yes — it's free, well designed, and has real note and highlight tools. For original-language work it isn't built for that job at all: no Strong's concordance, no Greek or Hebrew interlinear, no verse-level commentary pane. Pair it with Blue Letter Bible for the study side rather than expecting one app to do both.
What does Blue Letter Bible actually cost?
Nothing. It's fully free, ad-free, with no in-app purchases and no premium tier — Strong's numbers, the interlinear, the lexicon, and its commentary library are all included from install.
Do I need Logos if I already use Olive Tree?

Only if you've outgrown what Olive Tree's individually priced resources cover. Logos's real advantage is its subscription-wide resource library and the Greek/Hebrew syntax search on its Max tier — a scholar's toolset most casual study never reaches. Most people hit Olive Tree's or Blue Letter Bible's ceiling long before they hit Logos's.
Does FaithWall replace a study app?

No, and it isn't trying to. FaithWall has no notes, no lexicon, and no commentaries — it's a lock-screen layer that keeps a verse in view between the times you open a real study app. Think of it as the habit layer, not the study layer.
What's the cheapest way to get real Bible commentaries on an iPhone?

Blue Letter Bible, by a wide margin — its commentary library ships free with no paywall. Olive Tree and Bible Gateway both charge for their deeper commentary sets, and Logos's most-cited scholarly commentaries sit behind its highest subscription tier.
